segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Mrs Pike found the curate in the vestry on Tuesday, putting away the sacrament linen, and asked him for the banns of Margaret Selby and Robert Dene to be read on Sunday.

segments.speaker: Mr Silas Rowe
segments.text: I read banns when the two parties come to me and ask for them. Both of them. In this room.

segments.speaker: Mrs Honoria Pike
segments.text: I heard the engagement with my own ears in the porch, Mr Rowe, and so did forty people.

segments.speaker: Mr Silas Rowe
segments.text: I heard it from you as well, ma'am. That is precisely the difficulty.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: She went down the path convinced he was proud, which was a thing the parish had long since settled about him on less evidence.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the next ten days Mrs Pike arranged them. There was a walk to Nine Acres on Wednesday and cold mutton at the house on the green on Friday, and on Saturday the pair were sent to look at the lime trees for no reason anybody could name. Dene carried the music case without being asked. He told Margaret that the youngest Ludd boy had got through a whole page of Hollis's psalter aloud, and his ears went red telling it, and Margaret found she had stopped walking to listen.

segments.speaker: Miss Margaret Selby
segments.text: You are very proud of them.

segments.speaker: Mr Robert Dene
segments.text: I have forty pounds a year and twenty-two children. One of those numbers is worth boasting of.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: On the Thursday following, Margaret came to the schoolroom door with the singing books and heard Dene inside, talking to the schoolmaster from Bramdean, who had walked over about a stove.

segments.speaker: Mr Robert Dene
segments.text: The day her aunt takes the coach, I shall put an end to it. I have had the good of it and I never earned a shilling of it, and it cannot stand another week after she is gone.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Margaret set the books on the step and went home along the lane. He meant to be done with her the hour it stopped being necessary. She had known that from the first; she had agreed to it in Mrs Copp's parlour, in her own words. It was not to be borne that hearing it should be so different from saying it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: At dinner that evening she passed him the salt and nothing else. He asked whether the Hollis girls had paid at Michaelmas and she said they had. Mrs Pike beamed at the pair of them from the head of the table. Mrs Ferris looked at her niece over the top of her spectacles and said nothing at all, which was worse.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: At the gate he had perhaps four seconds, with two women watching from the lit window.

segments.speaker: Miss Margaret Selby
segments.text: Nothing whatever. You have done exactly what we agreed.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: She went in. Behind the glass, Mrs Pike remarked that it was very pretty to see young people say good night.
